contributions.headingText: Mantle cell lymphoma (MCL) is a mature B-cell neoplasm usually composed of monomorphic small to medium-sized lymphoid cells with irregular nuclear contours that commonly express CD5 and in > 95% of tumours carry the t(11;14)(q13;q32) translocation leading to cyclin D1 overexpression.
Conventional mantle cell lymphoma; leukaemic non-nodal mantle cell lymphoma

Lymph nodes are the most commonly involved site in conventional MCL (cMCL), although extranodal involvement is frequent. Subclinical tumour cell infiltration of the GI tract is common in patients with MCL {17001159; 12548600}. Superficial ulcers, large tumour masses, and diffuse thickening of the gastrointestinal mucosa may be seen {7657310}. Presentation as multiple intestinal polyps (multiple lymphomatous polyposis) is distinctive, although not specific for MCL {8659449; 8604811}. Circulating cells in leukaemic non-nodal MCL (nnMCL) may reversibly infiltrate extranodal inflammatory sites (e.g. Helicobacter pylori–associated gastritis) {24352646}.

Most patients present with stage III/IV disease with lymphadenopathy and bone marrow involvement. Extranodal involvement usually occurs in association with lymphadenopathy. nnMCL presents as isolated bone marrow and blood involvement, sometimes accompanied by splenomegaly; nodal dissemination may occur with clinical progression.
MCL accounts for 3–10% of all lymphoid neoplasms. It is more common in males than females (> 2:1), with a median patient age of about 60 years.

The t(11;14)(q13;q32) translocation between an IGH gene and CCND1 is present in > 95% of cases of MCL, and this is considered the primary genetic event. The translocation results in deregulated overexpression of CCND1 mRNA and the cyclin D1 protein. The cases of MCL lacking CCND1 translocation show CCND2 (~75%) or CCND3 translocations, usually with an IG partner, often either IGK or IGL [[Swerdlow SH, Campo E, Seto M, et al. Mantle cell lymphoma. In: Swerdlow SH, Campo E, Harris NL, et al., editors. WHO classification of tumours of haematopoietic and lymphoid tissues. Lyon (France): International Agency for Research on Cancer; 2017. p. 285-90. (WHO classification of tumours series, 4th rev. ed.; vol. 2). http://publications.iarc.fr/556.]].

cMCL shows complex karyotypes, particularly in blastoid/pleomorphic subtypes. nnMCL shows few genetic alterations other than t(11;14). Frequently mutated genes in cMCL include ATM (40–75%), KMT2D (14–18%), and NOTCH1 or NOTCH2 (5–12%) {29666114}. CDKN2A deletions/mutations (20–25%) in cMCL and TP53 mutations (15–35%) in both cMCL and nnMCL are associated with high proliferation and aggressive behaviour {28819011}.

There may be subclinical tumour cell infiltration of the GI tract or superficial ulcers, large tumour masses, and diffuse thickening of the gastrointestinal mucosa. Presentation as multiple intestinal polyps (multiple lymphomatous polyposis) is distinctive but not specific.

Classic MCL is a monomorphic proliferation of small-intermediate lymphoid cells with scant cytoplasm and irregular nuclei that have dispersed chromatin and inconspicuous nucleoli. The tumour may show a mantle zone and a nodular or diffuse growth pattern. Tumour cells may have a spectrum of cytological subtypes. The small cell subtype is more common in nnMCL and shows round nuclei mimicking chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, but without nucleolated cells. The blastoid subtype is characterized by intermediate-sized cells with round nuclei and finely dispersed chromatin, mimicking lymphoblasts, and numerous mitoses. The pleomorphic subtype shows large irregular nuclei with nucleoli.

Mantle cell neoplasia in situ is characterized by the presence of cyclin D1–positive cells restricted to the mantle zone of otherwise reactive follicles. When mantle cell neoplasia in situ is found incidentally, progression to overt MCL is uncommon {23999128}.

MCL cells express mature B-cell markers (CD20, CD79a), CD5, and CD43. CD10/BCL6 and CD23 are usually negative. Nuclear cyclin D1 is expressed in > 95% of MCLs, including those that are CD5-negative. SOX11 is expressed in cMCL but is negative in nnMCL. LEF1 is negative but may be expressed in the blastoid and pleomorphic subtypes. CD200 is negative in cMCL, but it is expressed in 40–90% of nnMCL cases {29666114}. The subset of cyclin D1–negative MCL shows the same morphology, phenotype, and clinical features as cyclin D1–positive cases, including SOX11 expression {23255553}.
The t(11;14)(q13;q32) translocation between an IGH gene and CCND1 is present in > 95% of cases of MCL, and it is a desirable diagnostic criterion if other features are absent.

Essential: diffuse, nodular to mantle zone proliferation of small to medium-sized cells with irregular nuclear contours, dispersed chromatin, and inconspicuous nucleoli – blastoid and pleomorphic subtypes will show different cytological features; B-cell neoplasm with expression of CD5 and cyclin D1; SOX11 often positive.

Desirable: morphological features suggestive of MCL and CD5-positive but cyclin D1–negative: diagnosis to be confirmed by SOX11 positivity and/or CCND2/3 translocations.
Lymphoid neoplasms are staged according to the Lugano classification, which has been adopted by the eighth edition of the Union for International Cancer Control (UICC) TNM classification {25113753}.

Proliferative activity is the most important independent prognostic parameter in MCL {26926679}. The Ki-67 proliferation index adds value to the Mantle Cell Lymphoma International Prognostic Index (MIPI) {17962512}. Genomic complexity confers poor outcome {29769262}.
